the recorded-offence cohort method follows offences recorded in a defined reporting period; outcomes are linked back to individual recorded crimes; the distribution changes as investigations receive outcomes over time.
recent cohorts are incomplete; cohort percentages require an extraction date.
the closed-period measure counts outcomes recorded in the reporting year; associated crimes may have been recorded in earlier years; the measure describes police activity across mixed crime cohorts.
closed-period volumes are not a same-cohort resolution rate; crime-recording dates must remain separate.

closed-period outcome rates can exceed 100 percent for some low-volume crimes; the technical annex calls these rates illustrative rather than true rates; the numerator can include outcomes for offences recorded in previous years.
rates above 100 percent are not impossible values to clip; the measure must not be interpreted as a probability.

closed-period rates compare outcomes recorded in a year with crimes recorded in the same year; the two groups are not necessarily the same offences; changes in recorded-crime volumes can change the illustrative rate.
volume-driven movement is not necessarily investigative-performance change; cross-period comparisons need cohort context.

timeliness measures elapsed time between offence recording and outcome assignment; it can be used as a proxy for investigative efficiency; the Home Office says it should not be considered a firm measure.
administrative timing affects the measure; timeliness is not a parcel safety score.

an outcome can be achieved before it is entered on the crime-recording system; recording delay affects measured timeliness; the technical annex distinguishes operational action from system implementation.
system timestamps do not always equal operational decision time; force processes may differ.

some outcomes measured as taking one to five days may have been actioned on the offence date; cannabis-warning administration is given as an example; later system assignment can create apparent elapsed days.
the example does not apply to every outcome; short elapsed time is not proof of same-day action.
a small number of forces submit monthly aggregated crime and outcome data using Crimsec4; the return is organised by notifiable offence; Crimsec4 differs from record-level Home Office Data Hub data.
aggregated returns cannot support record-level linkage; force coverage can change by edition.
Crimsec4 records an outcome in the month it is applied; the original offence can have occurred months earlier; outcome data for a month may not correspond to offences in that month or year.
application month must not be treated as offence month; aggregated monthly data cannot reconstruct exact case timelines.
Crimsec4 covers offences in the notifiable offence list; the list includes offences that could be tried by jury; it also includes some closely related summary offences.
notifiable crime is not all offending or all incidents; scope changes require offence-reference versioning.

the broader outcomes framework replaced the detections regime; the full framework was introduced in April 2014; the 2014 to 2015 bulletin was the first publication based entirely on the full framework.
pre-framework and full-framework data are not directly interchangeable; outcome definitions require period metadata.
open data on crime outcomes has been published since 2014 to 2015; following consultation it has been updated quarterly since October 2015; quarterly files are versioned statistical products.
quarterly publication does not imply stable historical values; each extraction must be pinned.
the recorded-quarter view links outcomes to individual crimes; it includes a category for investigations still open; a quarter's first publication is explicitly an incomplete picture.
open investigations later migrate to final outcomes; early-quarter distributions should not be ranked as final.
outcomes are published for offences recorded in the quarter; outcomes are also published for investigations closed in the quarter; the two fields answer different analytical questions.
the two measures must not be summed or substituted; cohort and closed-period semantics must be retained.

the open-data specification includes an Offence Code Expired field; the value X marks codes expired before April 2014; outcomes under such codes can relate only to offences recorded in previous years.
expired codes require historical mapping; X is not a missing-value marker.
the open-data outcome-type field uses numeric outcome codes; documented values include 1 to 18 and 20 to 22; outcome description and outcome group are separate fields.
code gaps must not be auto-filled; labels need the applicable reference table.
each open-data row contains a single count; columns identify time period offence and area; outcome description group and type further qualify the count.
a row is an aggregate cell rather than an incident record; duplicate-key checks require the full field set.
the supplementary outcomes metrics specification includes a value field; the value is published with no rounding applied; time period may be rolling annual or quarterly.
unrounded presentation does not remove source uncertainty; period type must remain attached.
an empty supplementary-metric value can mean suppressed due to low volumes; the reason is carried in reason_for_missing_data; suppression is an explicit missing state.
suppressed values must not be replaced by zero; suppression can affect comparability.
an empty supplementary-metric value can mean no data to calculate the field; this state is distinct from suppression; the reason is explicitly encoded.
no-data-to-calculate must not be treated as zero; the upstream missing input is not identified by this label alone.
